intro: The source attributes this Victor 88061 side to Caruso’s 1907 orchestral recording, unlike his 1902 piano-accompanied account. Its exact master is inferred from the catalogue rather than confirmed from a legible runout; the complete longer side remains one unaltered stream.
question: How does orchestral accompaniment frame Caruso’s phrasing?

sections.label: Central expansion
sections.mNote: analysis landmark, not an aligned word or score bar

cues.title: The orchestra replaces the piano
cues.text: This Victor side places orchestral accompaniment beneath Caruso’s tenor. Follow the relation between the singer’s line and the accompaniment, without assuming that the transfer preserves the original balance of the recording room.
cues.evidence: The Great 78 metadata and DAHR C-4317 identify tenor with orchestra and an acoustic recording: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/200006029. The microphone or horn balance is not measured.

cues.title: A marked early relaxation
cues.text: The early dramatic span relaxes into a quieter stretch before regaining weight. Listen for the continuity of the phrase across that contrast rather than treating it as silence.
cues.evidence: A boundary occurs at 0:40; relative level falls from −12.7 dB at 0:25 to −23.3 dB at 0:40, then rises again at 0:50. This does not locate an exact sung word.

cues.title: The first stronger expansion
cues.text: The next rise reaches a stronger recorded span, then releases. Compare the shape of that expansion with the later, broader crest on the same side.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 0:58, 1:02 and 1:10 surround the rise to −9.3 dB at 1:05. The later 1:40–1:55 span is stronger within this transfer.

cues.title: A broad late crest
cues.text: The central-late span holds its greater weight across several gestures. Listen through the whole crest, keeping the accompaniment audible in your attention as well as the tenor.
cues.evidence: The 1:40, 1:45, 1:50 and 1:55 windows are four of the report’s five highest; boundaries at 1:36 and 1:46 locate this broad passage.

cues.title: Beyond the compared passage
cues.text: The side continues after the excerpt used by the comparison map. Its later sound has less recorded weight; hear it on its own terms rather than stretching the shorter 1902 side to fill the remaining time.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary is 2:22, after the selected map endpoint of 139 seconds. The 2:20–2:25 windows are among the quietest; the stream continues to 195.9 seconds. No unverified word or cut is assigned here.

cues.title: The transfer’s last sound
cues.text: Near the end, the remaining sound diminishes towards the disc’s surface noise. The complete file duration includes this closing material and is not a measure of the shared excerpt’s pace.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −21.5 dB at 3:00 to −29.1 at 3:05 and −33.9 at 3:15. The comparison excludes this later continuation; onset counts are not treated as clean note detections.

transitions.title: The quieter span gains weight
transitions.how: The quieter early span gives way to a stronger expansion while tenor and orchestra remain together. The section marker follows a measured contour rather than a precisely identified syllable.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:58; level rises from −19.0 dB at 0:55 to −9.3 dB at 1:05.

transitions.title: The phrase develops a broader crest
transitions.how: The phrase gathers into a longer high-level span than the preceding brief rise. Keep following its direction across successive gestures rather than isolating one recorded peak.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:36; the following 1:40–1:55 windows are the strongest sustained span in the report.

transitions.title: The crest leaves a quieter continuation
transitions.how: The late high-level gestures are followed by a markedly quieter continuation. This material remains part of the unedited source, but lies outside the comparison excerpt.
transitions.evidence: Strong boundary at 2:22; level drops from −12.5 dB at 2:15 to −25.6 dB at 2:25. No compositional cut or orchestral entrance is inferred.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Orchestral accompaniment is documented, but no orchestra name, conductor or individual orchestral players are established by the cited sources.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Tenor with orchestral accompaniment; Italian; source describes acoustic recording
fields.note: IA describes an acoustic recording and identifies Victor/Victrola 88061. Attribution to the original C-4317 master is inferred through the catalogue, not confirmed by a legible runout. DAHR lists later electrically re-orchestrated dubs separately as CS-58966; this transfer has not been independently distinguished from every later reissue or dub by matrix inspection. Performing edition unknown.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Date of the original C-4317 acoustic session, applied through the source’s 1907 attribution and Victor 88061 catalogue identity. The transfer’s exact matrix is not independently confirmed; this is not a date for the physical pressing or transfer.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Place of the attributed original C-4317 session. No studio address is asserted, and the transfer’s exact matrix has not been independently confirmed.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The transferred label is identified in the IA metadata; the underlying master is Victor.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The physical pressing date is unknown; 1907 identifies the original recording and issue history, not this copy’s manufacture.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: DAHR identifies take 1 as the issued master for Victor 88061; take 2 was held. This identifies the master through the catalogue, not through inspection of a legible runout. IA’s matrix field repeats the catalogue number 88061 and is not accepted as the matrix.

fields.note: The item specifies 3.8, 2.3, 2.8 and 3.3 mil truncated-conical styli. The specific selected stylus and further restoration are not established. Playback audio remains unaltered.
